title: The Turin Horse - A Beautiful Apocalyptic Premonition

commenti.body:
> There is no redemption in this story, no speck of hope.

Certainly true, it's the bleakest possible view of reality. Tarr's previous films always had something to leaven the message, either some darkly comic character (eg the sidekick of Irimias in Satantango, who reacts to certain events on behalf of the viewer like Sancho Panza) or a character that provides a ray of light (like Janos in The Werckmeister Harmonies). In the Turin Horse everyone is trapped, even the gypsies. There's no running from the apocalypse. The entire narrative is trapped, turning round and round on itself.

I saw Tarr's films more or less as they came out, waiting eagerly for the next one. I found it very powerful that this final statement is the non plus ultra of the philosophy woven through all of his films. The fact that the actor who played the girl in Satantango returns seems an important part of this meta-content, the position of this film as the last word. In each appearance she represents to me innocence debased and destroyed. In the first film this is done by the (human) cynicism and corruption around her. In the later one it is simply the nature of reality. Before seeing TH I was disappointed to think it would be Tarr's last film but after seeing it I thought, well, yeah. There really is nothing to add.

I think the Nietzsche story is a fantastic simulacrum for this film and what it says. Because Nietzsche pontificates throughout his work about his ideals of power and strength, of embracing evil and suffering, even of being free from pity. I think Tarr shows us the vanity of all those things with the destitution and squalor that we see in the film. There us nothing any one of us can do in a situation as dire as this. We simply fall down and must weep at such a tragic sight. It's also significant that Nietzsche was vehemently anti-communist and anti-egalitarian.
